stem: A form has a "Save" button. Following Testing Library's guidance on query priority, which query should a test use to find it?
explanation: Testing Library recommends queries in the order users perceive the page: `getByRole` first (with a `name` option), then `getByLabelText`, placeholder, text and display value, then alt text and title, and `getByTestId` only as a last resort. Querying by role also checks accessibility for free: if `getByRole('button', { name: /save/i })` fails, a screen-reader user may not find the button either.
reference: Testing Library docs: About Queries (priority)

options.text: `screen.getByTestId('save-button')` after adding a `data-testid` to the button
options.why: Test IDs are the last resort: users and assistive tech never see them.

options.text: `screen.getByRole('button', { name: /save/i })`
options.why: Role plus accessible name is how users and screen readers find the control, so it is the top-priority query.

options.text: `container.querySelector('.save-btn')`
options.why: Class names are implementation details; a styling refactor would break the test without breaking the feature.

options.text: `screen.getByText('Save')`, which matches any element whose text is "Save"
options.why: It works, but it ignores the role, so a "Save" heading or label could match instead of the button.

stem: `screen.queryByText('Error')` returns `null` instead of throwing when nothing matches, which makes it the right query for asserting that an element is absent.
explanation: Use `getBy*` when the element must exist (the thrown error explains what was on the page), `queryBy*` when asserting absence, and `findBy*` when the element appears asynchronously. All three throw if more than one element matches; use the `*AllBy*` variants for lists.
reference: Testing Library docs: Types of Queries

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: queryBy* returns null on no match (and still throws on multiple matches), so `expect(screen.queryByText('Error')).not.toBeInTheDocument()` reads cleanly.

options.text: False
options.why: It is true: getBy* throws on no match, while queryBy* returns null so absence can be asserted.

stem: A card component needs a clickable "Delete" control. Which markup is accessible to keyboard and screen-reader users without extra work?
explanation: Native elements carry built-in semantics and behaviour. A `<button>` is in the tab order, exposes the button role, and turns Enter and Space into click events. Recreating that on a div needs `role`, `tabIndex={0}`, key handlers and focus styles, and is easy to get wrong. `type="button"` matters inside forms, where the default `type="submit"` would submit the form.
reference: MDN: The Button element; WAI-ARIA APG: Button pattern

options.text:
`
Delete
`
options.why: A div is not focusable, has no button role and does not respond to Enter or Space.

options.text: `Delete`
options.why: The role is announced, but the span still is not focusable and ignores Enter and Space unless you add tabIndex and key handlers.

options.text: `<button type="button" onClick={onDelete}>Delete</button>`
options.why: A native button is focusable, announced as a button, and fires click on Enter and Space for free.

options.text: `Delete` with no `href` attribute
options.why: An anchor without href is not focusable and is not exposed as a link or a button.

stem: Testing Library has three query prefixes: `getBy`, `queryBy` and a third one that returns a Promise and retries until the element appears or a timeout passes. Type that third prefix.
explanation: `findBy*` queries are `getBy*` wrapped in `waitFor`: they retry (default timeout 1000 ms) and resolve with the element, or reject if it never appears. Use them for UI that shows up after a fetch or other async work: `expect(await screen.findByText('Saved')).toBeInTheDocument()`.
reference: Testing Library docs: Types of Queries

explanation: Passing `value` makes an input controlled: React owns its value and re-applies `name` after each event. Without `onChange` (or `readOnly`), the user cannot change it, and React warns in development. Either add `onChange={(e) => setName(e.target.value)}`, use `readOnly`, or make it uncontrolled with `defaultValue`.
reference: react.dev: <input> (controlling an input with a state variable)

options.text: It updates normally; React syncs `name` from the DOM
options.why: React never reads the DOM back into state; only an onChange handler can update `name`.

options.text: The text stays "Ada", and React warns about `value` without `onChange`
options.why: A `value` prop makes the input controlled; with no handler to update state, React keeps resetting it.

options.text: The input becomes uncontrolled after the first keystroke and keeps whatever the user types
options.why: It stays controlled for its whole life because `value` is always a string.

options.text: React throws an error during render because controlled inputs require `defaultValue` as well
options.why: There is no such requirement, and `defaultValue` is for uncontrolled inputs.

stem: Match each React pattern with what it is.
explanation: All four share logic or state between components. HOCs and render props were the main tools before hooks; custom hooks now cover most logic reuse with less nesting. Compound components remain the go-to for flexible UI APIs such as tabs, menus and selects, usually built on context.
reference: react.dev: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks; patterns.dev

options.text: Compound components
Render props
Higher-order component (HOC)
Custom hook

prompts.text: A function that takes a component and returns a new component with extra behaviour
A component that calls a function prop to decide what to render
A group like `<Tabs>`, `<Tabs.List>` and `<Tabs.Panel>` that shares state implicitly
A `use…` function that packages stateful logic for any component to call

stem: Which markup lets a test find the input with `screen.getByLabelText('Email')`, and lets a screen reader announce it as "Email"?
explanation: A label is associated with a control either by wrapping it (`<label>Email <input /></label>`) or by `htmlFor` pointing at the input's `id`. `aria-labelledby` also works. Placeholders and descriptions do not provide a name. In reusable components, generate the id with `useId` so several instances on one page don't collide.
reference: react.dev: <label>; Testing Library: ByLabelText

options.text: `<label>Email</label><input id="email" />`
options.why: A label next to an input is not associated with it unless it wraps the input or uses htmlFor.

options.text: `<input placeholder="Email" />`
options.why: A placeholder is not a label: it disappears on input and getByLabelText does not use it.

options.text: `<label htmlFor="email">Email</label><input id="email" />`
options.why: In JSX the `for` attribute is written `htmlFor`; matching it to the input id associates the label.

options.text: `Email`
options.why: aria-describedby supplies a description, not the accessible name, so the input still has no label.

explanation: Since v14, every user-event interaction (`click`, `type`, `keyboard`, …) is async. Mark the test `async` and `await` each call: `await user.type(input, 'hi')`. Without it the assertion runs first, and you may also get act() warnings when the late updates land after the test.
reference: user-event docs: Setup and async APIs

options.text: `userEvent.setup()` must run in `beforeEach`
options.why: Calling setup inside the test is the recommended style.

options.text: user-event 14 calls return Promises, so the assertion runs before typing
options.why: Each key is dispatched asynchronously, so the test must `await user.type(...)` and be an async function.

options.text: Controlled inputs ignore user-event, so the test should use `fireEvent.change` instead
options.why: user-event works with controlled inputs; it fires the same events a real user would.

options.text: `toHaveValue` reads the `value` attribute, which React never updates for controlled inputs
options.why: toHaveValue reads the current value property, which does update.

stem: Which two statements about `screen.getByText(...)` are true? (Choose two.)
explanation: getBy*: exactly one match or throw. queryBy*: null on zero matches, throw on several. findBy*: async, retries until exactly one match or timeout. Each has an `*AllBy*` variant that returns arrays (getAllBy and findAllBy throw on zero matches; queryAllBy returns []).
reference: Testing Library docs: Types of Queries (summary table)

options.text: It throws if no element matches
options.why: getBy* fails loudly and prints the DOM, which makes the failure easy to debug.

options.text: It throws if more than one element matches
options.why: Single-element queries refuse to guess; use getAllByText for lists.

options.text: It retries for up to 1000 ms before giving up
options.why: That is findBy*. getBy* checks the DOM once, synchronously.

options.text: It returns `null` when nothing matches
options.why: That is queryBy*.

options.text: It returns an array of every matching element
options.why: That is getAllBy*.

explanation: An HOC returns a different component, so anything attached to the original (`Menu.Item`, `defaultProps`-style config, `displayName`) is missing on the wrapper. Copy what you need, set a `displayName` like `withTheme(Menu)` for DevTools, and prefer hooks or composition where possible to avoid the problem altogether.
reference: React legacy docs: Higher-Order Components (static methods must be copied)

options.text: Hooks inside an HOC strip static properties from the component during rendering
options.why: Hooks have nothing to do with statics; the property is simply never copied.

options.text: Statics only work on class components
options.why: Any function can carry properties; Menu.Item works fine on the original.

options.text: The HOC returns a new function, so `Item` must be copied onto `Themed`
options.why: Copy it explicitly (`Themed.Item = Menu.Item`) or use a helper such as hoist-non-react-statics.

options.text: Spreading `{...props}` overwrites `Item`, because statics are passed to children as props
options.why: Statics are properties of the component function, not props.

explanation: JSX decides by case: lowercase names (`<as>`, `<div>`) become strings, capitalised names (`<Comp>`) become variable references. The polymorphic pattern therefore assigns to a capitalised variable first: `const Comp = as ?? 'div'; return <Comp {...rest} />;`. This was checked with `renderToString`, which prints `<as>x</as>`.
reference: react.dev: Writing Markup with JSX; Your First Component (capitalisation)

options.why: JSX does not look up a lowercase tag in scope; it treats it as a literal element name.

options.text: `<as>x</as>`, since lowercase JSX tags are HTML tag names
options.why: `<as>` compiles to createElement("as"), so the prop value is ignored.

options.text: Nothing: `as` is reserved in JSX
options.why: `as` is not reserved; it simply becomes the string "as".

An HOC that spreads `{...props}` now forwards the ref automatically (verified: the ref pointed at the inner `<input>`). In React 18 the same code silently dropped the ref, so library code that supports both versions still uses `forwardRef`.
reference: react.dev: React 19 release (ref as a prop)

explanation: The fetch resolves after the test body finished, so React applies the state update outside any act scope and warns. The fix is to let the test observe the outcome: await a `findBy*` query (or `waitFor`) for the loaded UI, and mock the request (for example with MSW). That both removes the warning and tests the behaviour that matters.
reference: React Testing Library docs: Fix the "not wrapped in act(...)" warning (Kent C. Dodds)

options.text: Wrap `render` in `act(...)` yourself
options.why: RTL already wraps render and events in act; the stray update comes later.

options.text: Await the loaded UI, e.g. `await screen.findByText('Ada')`
options.why: The warning means state changed after the test stopped looking; awaiting the result keeps the update inside the test.

options.text: Silence it by setting `globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = false` in the test setup
options.why: That hides a real signal that the test ends before the component settles.

options.text: Replace `useEffect` with `useLayoutEffect` so the fetch resolves synchronously
options.why: Changing effect type does not make the network response synchronous.

stem: Put Testing Library's query types in its recommended priority order, highest first.
explanation: The guide groups queries as: accessible to everyone (`ByRole`, `ByLabelText`, `ByPlaceholderText`, `ByText`, `ByDisplayValue`), semantic queries (`ByAltText`, `ByTitle`), and test IDs (`ByTestId`) as the escape hatch. The higher a query sits, the closer it is to how users, including assistive-technology users, find things.
reference: Testing Library docs: About Queries (Priority)

options.text: `getByText`
`getByRole`
`getByAltText`
`getByLabelText`
`getByTestId`

stem: Put the steps of an accessible modal dialog interaction in order.
explanation: The WAI-ARIA dialog pattern moves focus into the dialog on open, keeps it trapped there while open (native `<dialog>` with `showModal()` does this, or a focus trap), closes on Escape, and returns focus to the element that opened it so keyboard users don't lose their place.
reference: WAI-ARIA APG: Dialog (Modal) pattern

options.text: Tab and Shift+Tab cycle focus only within the dialog
The user activates the "Edit profile" button
The user presses Escape and the dialog closes
Focus moves to the first focusable element inside the dialog
Focus returns to the "Edit profile" button

stem: A reusable `<EmailField />` renders `<label htmlFor="email">` and `<input id="email">`. A page renders it twice (billing and shipping). What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
explanation: IDs must be unique per document. With duplicates, clicking the second label focuses the first input and `getByLabelText` finds two elements. `useId()` returns a stable, unique id per component instance that is identical in server and client renders, which is exactly what label/aria associations need. Don't use it for list keys.
reference: react.dev: useId

options.text: Nothing: React scopes ids per instance
options.why: React does no such scoping; ids are global to the document.

options.text: Ids repeat, so both labels target the first input; use `useId()`
options.why: useId gives each instance a unique id that also matches between server and client rendering.

options.text: The second input fails to render because React refuses to create duplicate ids
options.why: React renders duplicates silently; the browser just resolves htmlFor to the first match.

options.text: Use `Math.random()` in render to create the id, which keeps every instance unique
options.why: Random ids differ between server and client, causing hydration mismatches, and change on every render.

stem: A `<Tabs>` component shares the active tab with `<Tabs.Tab>` and `<Tabs.Panel>` through context. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)
explanation: Context-based compound components let the parent own state and expose it to any descendant, so markup stays flexible. Consumers still re-render on each change, which is usually fine; split contexts or memoise the value if it matters. A custom hook like `useTabsContext()` that throws when the provider is missing gives a much better error than an undefined crash.
reference: Kent C. Dodds: Compound Components with React Hooks; react.dev: useContext

options.text: Consumers can wrap tabs in their own layout elements, because context reaches any descendant
options.why: Context does not care how deeply children are nested, unlike cloning direct children.

options.text: A `Tabs.Tab` rendered outside `<Tabs>` reads the context default, so a hook that throws a clear error is a common guard
options.why: Throwing "Tabs.Tab must be used inside <Tabs>" turns silent misuse into an obvious error.

options.text: Context-based compound components only work with class components
options.why: Function components and hooks are the usual way to build them.

options.text: Using context means that changing the active tab re-renders none of the tabs
options.why: Every consumer of the changed context value re-renders.

options.text: The parent must pass `active` and `onSelect` props to each child with `cloneElement`
options.why: That is the older cloneElement approach, which context replaces.

explanation: renderHook stores the hook's latest return value on `result.current`, which is a new object after every render. Destructuring captures a snapshot from that moment, exactly like a closure over render-time props. Verified: the destructured `count` is 0 while `result.current.count` is 1.
reference: React Testing Library API: renderHook

options.text: `act` must be awaited, so the increment has not happened yet
options.why: A synchronous state update inside a sync act is flushed before act returns.

options.text: `count` is a snapshot of the first render; read `result.current.count`
options.why: `result.current` is replaced on every render, while the destructured `count` stays 0.

options.text: renderHook does not re-render hooks after state updates, so the count never changes
options.why: It does re-render; result.current.count becomes 1.

options.text: `increment` is a stale closure, so it always sets the count back to its initial value
options.why: Even a "stale" increment updates state; the problem is reading an old snapshot of count.

explanation: waitFor re-runs its callback on an interval and on DOM mutations until it stops throwing. Any side effect inside it, such as a click, a fetch or a `setState`, can repeat an unknown number of times, which can make "Items: 1" impossible or flaky. Keep the callback free of side effects, ideally to a single assertion: `await user.click(add); expect(await screen.findByText('Items: 1')).toBeInTheDocument();`.
reference: Kent C. Dodds: Common mistakes with React Testing Library

options.text: waitFor callbacks must be async functions, so the click never runs at all
options.why: waitFor accepts sync callbacks and runs them repeatedly.

options.text: waitFor re-runs the callback, so it may click many times; click outside it
options.why: Move the click out and await it, then `await waitFor(() => expect(...))` or use findBy.

options.text: waitFor cannot contain expect calls; it only accepts queries that return elements
options.why: Assertions inside waitFor are the standard use.

options.text: getByText throws inside waitFor, which aborts it immediately instead of retrying
options.why: Throwing is exactly what makes waitFor retry until the timeout.

explanation: Negative assertions pass vacuously: "Invalid emial" (typo) matches nothing, so the test passes whether or not the real message is gone. Prove the element exists before asserting it disappears. `waitForElementToBeRemoved` enforces this; verified, it throws "The element(s) given to waitForElementToBeRemoved are already removed…" when nothing matches at the start.
reference: Testing Library docs: waitForElementToBeRemoved

options.text: Swap `queryByText` for `getByText`, so that a missing element throws
options.why: With getByText, a correct component would also throw once the message is gone.

options.text: Assert it appears, then `await waitForElementToBeRemoved(...)` with the right text
options.why: This also exposes the typo: the helper throws if the element is not present when it starts waiting.

options.text: Wrap the assertion in `act()` so React flushes the pending state update first
options.why: Flushing changes nothing: the query text never matches anything.

options.text: Increase the timeout of the test so that the asynchronous validation has time to finish
options.why: Waiting longer cannot help an assertion that is vacuously true.

stem: A test enables Vitest fake timers to check a debounced search, and then `await user.type(input, 're')` never resolves. Which two changes fix the hang? (Choose two.)
explanation: By default user-event pauses between actions with `setTimeout(…, 0)` (the `delay` option). Under fake timers that timeout never fires, so the promise hangs. Either tell user-event how to advance your fake clock (`advanceTimers`) or skip the delays (`delay: null`). Then advance time for the debounce yourself, e.g. `vi.advanceTimersByTime(300)` inside act if needed.
reference: user-event docs: Options (advanceTimers, delay)

options.text: Create the user with `userEvent.setup({ advanceTimers: vi.advanceTimersByTime })`
options.why: user-event waits on timers between actions; this lets it advance the fake clock itself.

options.text: Create the user with `userEvent.setup({ delay: null })`
options.why: With no delay between actions, user-event never waits on a timer at all.

options.text: Drop the `await` so that user-event runs synchronously under fake timers
options.why: The calls are still async; skipping await just races the assertions.

options.text: Call `vi.runAllTimers()` once before `userEvent.setup()`
options.why: Nothing is scheduled yet at that point; the hang starts during typing.

options.text: Switch every interaction to `fireEvent`, which is the only API that works with fake timers
options.why: fireEvent avoids the hang but drops realistic event sequences; user-event works fine once configured.

stem: A headless `useDropdown` hook supports the "state reducer" pattern so consumers can change its behaviour. Which implementation lets a consumer keep the menu open after an item is selected?
explanation: The state reducer pattern (popularised by Downshift) inverts control over transitions: the hook proposes the next state, and the consumer's reducer can accept, alter or replace it per action type. Consumers override just the edge cases, such as "stay open on select", without reimplementing the hook. Controlled props are the complementary pattern when a consumer wants to own a piece of state entirely.
reference: Kent C. Dodds: The State Reducer Pattern with React Hooks

options.text: The hook calls `props.stateReducer(state, action)` and ignores the return value, logging it instead
options.why: If the return value is ignored, the consumer cannot change any outcome.

options.text: The hook exposes `setState` directly, so the consumer can reopen the menu in an effect after each select
options.why: Patching state after the fact causes a visible close-then-open flicker and a wasted render.

options.text: It runs its own reducer, then uses `props.stateReducer(state, { ...action, changes })`
options.why: The consumer sees the proposed changes and can return a modified state, e.g. keeping `isOpen: true` on select.

options.text: The hook accepts an `isOpen` prop, and only that prop, so the consumer fully controls the menu at all times
options.why: That is the controlled-prop pattern: valid, but it forces consumers to own all state, not just tweak one transition.

stem: A headless `useToggle` hook offers a prop getter. A consumer writes `<button {...getToggleProps({ onClick: track })}>` and finds that `track` runs but the toggle no longer works. Which getter is correct?
explanation: Prop getters exist to merge consumer props with the hook's props safely. Event handlers must be composed (call both), not overwritten by spread order. The `defaultPrevented` check is a common escape hatch that lets consumers cancel the built-in behaviour.
reference: Kent C. Dodds: How to give rendering control to users with prop getters

options.text: `(props) => ({ 'aria-expanded': on, onClick: toggle, ...props })`
options.why: Spreading props last overwrites the internal onClick with the consumer's, so toggle never runs.

options.text: `(props) => ({ ...props, 'aria-expanded': on, onClick: toggle })`
options.why: Now the hook wins and the consumer's track handler is silently dropped.

options.text: `({ onClick, ...rest } = {}) => ({ 'aria-expanded': on, ...rest, onClick: (e) => { onClick?.(e); if (!e.defaultPrevented) toggle(); } })`
options.why: Both handlers run, and the consumer can opt out of the toggle by calling preventDefault.

options.text: `(props) => ({ 'aria-expanded': on, onClick: props.onClick ?? toggle })`
options.why: It runs one or the other, never both.

stem:
After an async save, the app shows "Profile saved". Screen-reader users hear nothing. The code renders `{saved &&

Profile saved

}`. What is the most reliable fix?
explanation:
Assistive tech registers live regions when they appear and then announces changes to their content. If the region and its text are inserted in the same update, many screen-reader and browser combinations stay silent. Keep the container mounted (`

{saved ? 'Profile saved' : ''}

`), use `role="status"` (polite) for confirmations and `role="alert"` (assertive) for urgent errors.
reference: MDN: ARIA live regions

options.text:
Add `aria-live="assertive"` to the `

`, because `role="status"` alone is never announced
options.why: role="status" already implies a polite live region; the problem is when the region is created.

options.text: Keep an empty `role="status"` element mounted and change only its text
options.why: Screen readers watch existing live regions for changes; a region inserted with its text already inside is often not announced.

options.text: Move focus to the message on every save
options.why: Stealing focus for a status message disrupts the user; live regions exist for exactly this case.

options.text: Use `aria-hidden="true"` on the rest of the page while the message is visible
options.why: Hiding content does not trigger an announcement and can make the page unusable.

stem: In a single-page app, keyboard and screen-reader users report that nothing happens when they follow a link, even though the new page renders. What is the standard fix?
explanation: On a full page load, screen readers announce the new title and start from the top. Client-side routing swaps DOM without that signal, and focus stays on a link that may no longer exist. Moving focus to the `<h1>` (made programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`) or announcing the route change restores the cue. Next.js's App Router includes a route announcer for this reason.
reference: Gatsby: What we learned from accessible client-side routing user testing; Next.js docs: Accessibility

options.text: Call `window.location.reload()` after each client-side navigation
options.why: That throws away the SPA's benefits and state.

options.text: Focus the new page's `<h1>` (with `tabIndex={-1}`) or announce the route
options.why: Browsers announce full page loads automatically; SPAs must do it themselves.

options.text: Add `autoFocus` to every link so focus stays where the user clicked
options.why: Focus staying on the old link is the problem: users don't learn the page changed.

options.text: Set `aria-live="polite"` on `<body>` so the whole new page is read aloud
options.why: That would read huge amounts of content on every update.

stem:
Why does `screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' })` fail for this markup?

```jsx
<button aria-label="Remove item">Delete</button>
```
explanation: The accessible name algorithm prefers `aria-labelledby`, then `aria-label`, then content. So screen readers announce "Remove item, button" while sighted users see "Delete", which also breaks voice control ("click Delete") and violates WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name. Verified: `name: 'Delete'` fails and `name: 'Remove item'` matches. Make the visible text part of the label, or drop the aria-label.
reference: W3C: Accessible Name and Description Computation; WCAG 2.5.3

options.text: getByRole only matches elements that have an explicit `role` attribute
options.why: Implicit roles from native elements are matched; `<button>` has role button.

options.text: Its accessible name is the `aria-label`, which overrides the text
options.why: In the name computation, aria-label wins over text content.

options.text: The `name` option must be a regular expression, not a string
options.why: Strings are matched exactly against the accessible name; regexes are optional.

options.text: Text inside a button is not part of its accessible name in jsdom
options.why: It is, when no aria-label or aria-labelledby is present.

stem: Which three statements about snapshot testing React components are accurate? (Choose three.)
explanation: Snapshots are cheap change detectors, not specifications. They work best when small and intentional (inline snapshots, serialised data rather than whole trees). Behaviour and accessibility are better covered by role-based queries and user-event interactions that fail for a reason a reviewer can understand.
reference: Jest docs: Snapshot Testing (best practices); Kent C. Dodds: Effective Snapshot Testing

options.text: Large snapshots are often updated with `-u` without review, so they stop catching regressions
options.why: Big diffs train reviewers to accept them blindly.

options.text: They catch unintended changes to rendered output, such as a dropped attribute or class
options.why: Any change to the serialised markup fails the test.

options.text: Small, focused inline snapshots (`toMatchInlineSnapshot`) are easier to review than whole-page snapshots
options.why: The expected output sits next to the test and stays small enough to read.

options.text: A passing snapshot proves the component behaves correctly when the user interacts with it
options.why: Snapshots record output at one moment; they assert nothing about behaviour.

options.text: Snapshots are a good replacement for accessibility checks, since they include all ARIA attributes
options.why: Seeing attributes in a snapshot is not the same as checking names, roles and focus behaviour.

explanation: Anything module-scoped in test setup is shared state. A shared QueryClient keeps cached queries between tests, so a later test may render cached data instead of hitting its mock. Create the client inside a `createWrapper()` function per test, and disable retries so failure states don't wait through retry delays.
reference: TanStack Query docs: Testing

options.text: The wrapper must be passed as `render(<Wrapper><Todos /></Wrapper>)`; the `wrapper` option is ignored for providers
options.why: The wrapper option is the documented way to supply providers.

options.text: One module-level client shares its cache between tests; create a new `QueryClient` (with `retry: false`) per test
options.why: Cached data from one test leaks into the next, so results depend on run order.

options.text: TanStack Query cannot run under jsdom, so these tests must use a real browser
options.why: It runs fine in jsdom; its own docs show this setup.

stem: In React 19, a test renders `<ErrorBoundary><Boom /></ErrorBoundary>`, where `Boom` throws during render. The fallback appears. What else happens?
explanation: React 19 replaced the duplicate logging of React 18 with a single report per error: caught errors go to `onCaughtError` (which defaults to `console.error`), uncaught ones to `onUncaughtError`. In tests, spy on and silence `console.error` around the boundary test, and assert on the fallback UI, not the log.
reference: react.dev: React 19 release (error handling), createRoot options

options.text: The error is rethrown after the fallback renders, so the test fails unless it is wrapped in `expect(...).toThrow()`
options.why: Caught errors are not rethrown; the test continues normally.

options.text: React still logs the caught error once with `console.error`, so tests often stub it
options.why: Verified in React 19.3: the fallback shows and console.error is called once.

options.text: Nothing is logged, because errors handled by a boundary are swallowed silently in React 19
options.why: React 19 reports caught errors through onCaughtError, which logs by default.

options.text: The boundary catches the error only if the test uses `act` explicitly, otherwise the render throws
options.why: RTL's render already runs inside act, and boundaries work the same either way.

stem:
How many elements does `screen.getAllByRole('listitem')` return for this list? Type a number. ```jsx
  • A
  • B
  • C
  • D
```
explanation: ByRole queries exclude elements that are inaccessible (removed from the accessibility tree) by default: the `hidden` attribute and `display: none` both qualify. So only A and D match. Pass `{ hidden: true }` to include them. Verified with jsdom and Testing Library: 2 items.
reference: Testing Library docs: ByRole (hidden option)

stem: Match each query variant with its behaviour when it finds no matching element.
explanation: The prefix tells you the failure mode. Only `queryBy`/`queryAllBy` tolerate absence (null and [] respectively); `getAllBy` also throws on zero matches, and `findAllBy` rejects. This is why `queryBy` is the one to use with `.not.toBeInTheDocument()`.
reference: Testing Library docs: Types of Queries

explanation: React compares element types by identity during reconciliation. `withAutosave(ProfileEditor)` returns a fresh function every time Page renders, so React sees a new type, unmounts the old subtree (losing state, DOM and focus) and mounts a new one. Apply HOCs once at module level: `const Editor = withAutosave(ProfileEditor);` outside the component.
reference: React legacy docs: Higher-Order Components (don't use HOCs inside render); react.dev: Preserving and Resetting State

options.text: `withAutosave` debounces onChange, which resets the input between keystrokes
options.why: Debouncing would delay saving, not wipe the input's DOM and focus.

options.text: Calling the HOC in render makes a new component type, so React remounts it
options.why: A different function identity means a different element type, so all state and DOM inside are thrown away.

options.text: HOCs cannot receive controlled `value` props, so the input falls back to uncontrolled mode
options.why: HOCs pass props through like any component.

options.text: useState inside Page resets on each keystroke because Page re-renders
options.why: Re-rendering keeps Page's own state; it is the child type that changes.

explanation: RTL renders into a div appended to `document.body` and returns it as `container`. Portalled content becomes a sibling of that div, not a child. Querying via `screen` (document.body) is the recommended default anyway, because it matches what the user sees regardless of where React mounts DOM.
reference: Testing Library docs: render (container), screen

options.text: Portals don't render in jsdom
options.why: Portals render fine in jsdom.

options.text: The portal renders outside `container`; query with `screen` instead
options.why: screen is bound to document.body, so it sees portalled content. Verified: within(container) throws, screen finds it.

options.text: The dialog role is only exposed once the modal receives focus, so focus it first
options.why: Roles do not depend on focus.

options.text: `within` cannot be used with RTL containers; it only works on elements returned by queries
options.why: within accepts any element, including container; the dialog just isn't inside it.

explanation: `Children.map` plus `cloneElement` only reaches immediate children, so any wrapper (a div, a fragment, a custom component) breaks the implicit contract. The div here even receives unknown props, which React warns about for DOM elements. React's docs list this as a pitfall of cloneElement; context-based compound components work at any depth.
reference: react.dev: cloneElement (pitfalls and alternatives)

options.text: `Children.map` skips children that are DOM elements, so no props are added at all
options.why: It maps over the div just fine; that is precisely the problem.

options.text: cloneElement copies props to every nested descendant, so both tabs receive `active: true`
options.why: cloneElement touches only the element it is given, not its children.

options.text: Only the div is cloned, so the props land on it, never on the tabs
options.why: cloneElement sees one level deep; context-based compound components avoid this.

options.text: Cloned props are dropped without a `key`
options.why: Keys affect reconciliation, not whether cloned props apply.

stem: A `<Toggle>` supports both controlled (`on`) and uncontrolled (`defaultOn`) use. It decides on every render: `const isControlled = props.on !== undefined`. What bug does this allow, and how do well-designed components handle it?
explanation: A component should be either controlled or uncontrolled for its whole lifetime. Deriving the mode each render lets an accidental `undefined` (a missing field in parent state, say) flip it to uncontrolled, where it resumes from whatever internal state it last had. Libraries such as Radix and Downshift capture the mode on first render (a ref) and log a development warning if it changes, mirroring React's own warning for `<input>`.
reference: react.dev: <input> (controlled vs uncontrolled pitfalls)

options.text: None: re-checking each render is the correct way to let parents switch modes at will
options.why: Switching modes mid-life makes the source of truth jump between parent and child, which loses state.

options.text: A later `on={undefined}` silently flips it to uncontrolled; lock the mode at mount
options.why: Native inputs do the same: React warns when an input switches between controlled and uncontrolled.

options.text: Controlled mode crashes when `on` is `false`, because `false !== undefined` is false
options.why: `false !== undefined` is true, so false is correctly treated as controlled.

options.text: The component must use `useEffect` to copy `props.on` into state, which fixes the switch
options.why: Mirroring props into state adds a render of lag and creates two sources of truth.

explanation: jsdom computes styles only from inline styles and stylesheets actually inserted into its document; your CSS bundle is not there. So visibility that depends on class names cannot be tested in jsdom (verified: `toBeVisible` passes on an element with a `hidden` class). Use the `hidden` attribute or conditional rendering (which jsdom understands), or test visual states in a real browser with Playwright or Vitest browser mode.
reference: jest-dom docs: toBeVisible; jsdom docs: CSS limitations

options.text: `toBeVisible` ignores styles entirely
options.why: It does check computed display, visibility, opacity and the hidden attribute.

options.text: jsdom doesn't load the app's CSS, so the `hidden` class hides nothing
options.why: Class-based hiding is invisible to jsdom; the first assertion should have been `not.toBeVisible()`, which would fail.

options.text: user-event clicks before React applies the class, so both checks happen in the visible state
options.why: Timing is not the issue; the class never hides anything in jsdom.

options.text: Tailwind classes only apply after hydration, and RTL renders without hydrating
options.why: Hydration has nothing to do with whether CSS is loaded.

stem:
A "Submit" button is disabled with `style={{ pointerEvents: 'none' }}` while a form is invalid. What do these two test approaches do?

```jsx
await user.click(submit);     // user-event 14
fireEvent.click(submit);       // fireEvent
```
explanation: user-event simulates what a real user can do, including the `pointer-events` check, so it errors with "Unable to perform pointer interaction as the element has `pointer-events: none`". fireEvent just dispatches a DOM event, so a test using it would pass while real users can't click. Better still, use the `disabled` attribute, which both blocks clicks and is announced to assistive tech; disable the check with `pointerEventsCheck: 0` only when you deliberately need to.
reference: user-event docs: Options (pointerEventsCheck)

options.text: Both call the onClick handler, because neither looks at CSS
options.why: user-event checks pointer-events before dispatching.

options.text: `user.click` throws on `pointer-events: none`; `fireEvent.click` runs the handler
options.why: Verified: user-event refuses the interaction, fireEvent ran onClick once.

options.text: Neither calls the handler, since jsdom implements pointer-events hit testing for both
options.why: fireEvent dispatches straight to the element with no hit testing.

options.text: user.click silently does nothing, while fireEvent throws an error about the style
options.why: It is the other way round: user-event throws, fireEvent does not care.

explanation: `createRoot(...).render()` schedules work rather than committing immediately. `act` (exported from `react` in React 19) makes React flush all pending work, effects and microtasks before your assertions. RTL wraps `render`, `fireEvent` and user-event in act for you; a hand-rolled helper must do it itself, and the `IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT` flag is what makes React warn when it doesn't.
reference: react.dev: act

options.text: "hello", because `root.render` commits synchronously in React 19
options.why: Concurrent roots schedule work; nothing is committed when render returns.

options.text: An empty string and an act() warning; `await act(...)` flushes the render
options.why: Verified in React 19.3: textContent is "" after render, and act flushes the update.

options.text: An empty string, and the update is lost until the next call to `root.render`
options.why: The update is only scheduled, not lost; it commits later or when act flushes.

options.text: "hello", but only because jsdom runs React's scheduler synchronously
options.why: jsdom has no influence on React's scheduling.

stem: A button has handlers for each event below. Put them in the order they fire during `await user.click(button)` (user-event 14).
explanation: user-event models a real pointer press: pointer events come first, then the compatibility mouse event; the button receives focus as part of mousedown's default action; the release fires pointerup then mouseup; and click comes last. Verified by logging React handlers under jsdom: PointerDown, MouseDown, Focus, PointerUp, MouseUp, Click. fireEvent.click would fire only the click.
reference: user-event docs: pointer API; UI Events specification

options.text: focus
pointerdown
pointerup
mousedown
mouseup
click

explanation: `user.type` clicks the element first, which by default places the cursor at the end of the current value, then sends each key. Two Backspaces remove "o" and "l", leaving "hel", and "X" makes "helX". Verified with user-event 14.6. Use `initialSelectionStart`/`initialSelectionEnd`, or `user.clear()` first, when you need a different starting point.
reference: user-event docs: type (initialSelectionStart)

stem: Which two statements about ARIA live regions are correct? (Choose two.)
explanation: Use `role="status"` (polite) for confirmations and `role="alert"` (assertive) sparingly for urgent, time-sensitive errors. Mount the region early and update its content. Live regions are one of the few places where seemingly harmless re-rendering choices (conditional mounting) change what users hear.
reference: MDN: ARIA live regions; WAI-ARIA 1.2: alert role

options.text: `role="alert"` behaves as an assertive live region, so it can interrupt what the screen reader is currently saying
options.why: alert implies aria-live="assertive" and aria-atomic="true".

options.text: Changing the text of a live region that is already in the DOM is announced more reliably than inserting a new region with text
options.why: Assistive tech must observe the region before its content changes.

options.text: `aria-live="polite"` waits until the page has fully loaded before making any announcements
options.why: Polite waits for the user to be idle, not for page load.

options.text: Content inside an `aria-hidden="true"` live region is still announced when it changes
options.why: aria-hidden removes it from the accessibility tree, so nothing is announced.

options.text: Every React state update inside a live region is announced, even when the text stays the same
options.why: Only actual content changes in the accessibility tree trigger announcements.

stem: An `<ErrorBoundary>` wraps a dashboard. Which two kinds of errors will it NOT catch? (Choose two.)
explanation: Boundaries catch errors during rendering, in lifecycle methods and effects of the tree below them (not in themselves). Errors in event handlers and arbitrary async callbacks don't pass through React's rendering, so catch them yourself, then store the error in state and throw it during render (the pattern behind `useErrorBoundary`/`showBoundary` in react-error-boundary) to show the fallback. Verified: a throwing onClick left the fallback hidden.
reference: react.dev: Catching rendering errors with an error boundary

options.text: An error thrown inside a button's `onClick` handler
options.why: Event handlers run outside rendering, so the error goes to the global handler instead.

options.text: A rejected promise from a `fetch` in a `setTimeout` callback that is never fed back into React
options.why: Async code outside rendering is invisible to boundaries unless you rethrow during render.

options.text: An error thrown while rendering a deeply nested child component
options.why: Render errors anywhere below the boundary are exactly what it catches.

options.text: An error thrown inside a child's `useEffect`
options.why: Errors in effects of descendants are caught by the nearest boundary.

options.text: An error thrown in a child's class lifecycle method such as `componentDidMount`
options.why: Lifecycle errors in descendants are caught too.

stem: Opening a native `<dialog>` with `dialog.showModal()` makes the content outside the dialog inert (unfocusable and hidden from assistive tech) and lets Escape close it, without a hand-written focus trap.
explanation: The native modal dialog handles the hard parts of the modal pattern: top-layer rendering, inertness of everything else, Escape to close, and focus moving into the dialog. React code still decides what to do on close (for example restoring focus to the trigger in older browsers). Note that jsdom does not implement `showModal`, so test this behaviour in a real browser. For custom overlays, the `inert` attribute (supported as a boolean prop since React 19) achieves the same background effect.
reference: MDN: <dialog> element; HTML spec: modal dialogs and inert

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: modal dialogs make the rest of the document inert, render in the top layer, and close on Escape.

options.text: False
options.why: It is true for showModal(); only dialog.show() opens a non-modal dialog without making the page inert.

stem: A team refactors `Counter` from `useState` to `useReducer` without changing its UI. Which two tests keep passing without edits? (Choose two.)
explanation: Tests that interact like a user and assert on what users perceive survive refactors; tests that reach into hooks or internal state break whenever implementation changes, even when nothing is wrong. That is the core idea behind "the more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you".
reference: Testing Library: Guiding Principles; Kent C. Dodds: Testing Implementation Details

options.text: A test that clicks the "Increment" button via `getByRole` and expects the text "Count: 1"
options.why: It exercises behaviour through the UI, which did not change.

options.text: A test that checks the button with accessible name "Increment" is enabled
options.why: Roles, names and states are part of the public contract, not the implementation.

options.text: A test that spies on `React.useState` and asserts it was called with `0`
options.why: useState is no longer called, so the spy fails.

options.text: A test that mocks `useReducer` to return `[{ count: 5 }, vi.fn()]` and expects "Count: 5"
options.why: It encodes the new internals; the old version of this test would have mocked useState instead.

options.text: An Enzyme-style test that reads the component's internal `count` state directly
options.why: Internal state shape is exactly what the refactor changed.

explanation: In browsers, `maxLength` constrains what users type or paste, not what scripts assign to `.value`. fireEvent.change sets the value property and dispatches an event, so a test using it could "prove" a 6-character value is accepted, which no real user could produce. user-event simulates keystrokes with the browser's constraints. Prefer user-event so tests fail when users would hit a wall, and validate on the server anyway.
reference: MDN: maxlength attribute; user-event docs: Introduction (fireEvent vs user-event)

options.text: Both see "abc", since the browser enforces maxLength for any value change
options.why: maxLength limits user input only; setting value programmatically ignores it.

options.text: A sees "abcdef" and B sees "abc": only user-event honours maxLength
options.why: Verified: fireEvent.change produced "abcdef", user.type produced "abc".

options.text: Both see "abcdef", because jsdom does not implement maxLength at all
options.why: user-event applies maxLength while typing, so Test B stops at three characters.

options.text: Test A sees "abc" and Test B sees "abcdef"
options.why: It is the reverse: fireEvent bypasses the limit and user-event honours it.
